entry.title: Drawing digits in the air with two ultrasonic sensors

link.title: Drawing digits in the air with two ultrasonic sensors

entry.content:
Move a pen through the air in front of two ultrasonic sensors and a web page draws its trail as you go. Four seconds after the first point, a neural network says which digit you wrote.

The Ultrasonic tab after reading a 2. Left: the 10 cm drawing area, with its edges in mm. Right: the 28×28 image the network received and its probability for each digit. This trail came from a script that sends traced points as sensor readings (see What it cannot do yet).

Why build this

It’s a teaching project. Every part is small: the firmware is 54 lines, the server 153, the training script 146, and the web page is one HTML file. Nothing hides in a library. The network is plain NumPy and the sensor readings travel as plain text, so a student can read every part in an afternoon, and every part has something to measure.

The project crosses four subjects that are usually taught apart:

  • Electronics: time of flight, logic levels, a voltage divider, timing.
  • Networking: WiFi, IP addresses, UDP ports, a firewall.
  • Signal processing: noise, spikes, a median filter, a low-pass filter, and the lag each one costs.
  • Machine learning: a dataset, a network trained from scratch, backpropagation by hand, overfitting, and what happens when real inputs don’t look like the training data.

The apparatus

Two HC-SR04 sensors at right angles. The one on the Y axis measures the object's x, the one on the X axis measures its y. The object is tracked only where both ~15° beams overlap.

An HC-SR04 sends a burst of 40 kHz sound when its TRIG pin gets a 10 µs pulse, then holds its ECHO pin high until the echo comes back. The distance follows from the time the pin stays high, \(t\), and the speed of sound, \(v\):

\[d = \frac{v\,t}{2}, \qquad v \approx 343\ \text{m/s at } 20\,^\circ\text{C}\]

The sound goes there and back, hence the 2. That is about 5.8 µs of echo per millimetre, and it is all the firmware needs:

int readMm(int trig, int echo) {
  digitalWrite(trig, HIGH);
  delayMicroseconds(10);
  digitalWrite(trig, LOW);
  // ~5.8 us of echo per mm of distance, plus up to ~3 ms before some modules raise ECHO
  unsigned long us = pulseIn(echo, HIGH, MAX_MM * 6 + 3000);
  return us ? us * 343 / 2000 : -1;  // sound at 343 m/s (20 °C), there and back
}

Three details of the circuit and the timing are worth a lesson each:

  • Logic levels. The HC-SR04 runs on 5 V and so does its ECHO output, but the ESP32-S3’s pins take 3.3 V. A divider with 1 kΩ from ECHO to the pin and 2 kΩ from the pin to ground brings it down to \(5 \times \frac{2}{1+2} \approx 3.3\) V. TRIG works from 3.3 V as it is.
  • Crosstalk. The two beams cross, so one sensor can hear the other’s ping. The firmware pings them in turn and pauses 25 ms after each, which caps the rate at about 16 pairs of readings per second.
  • Beam width. A beam about 15° wide is about 50 mm across at 200 mm, so the zone both sensors cover is small. I set the drawing area to 150–250 mm on both axes: a 10 cm square.
HC-SR04 pin ESP32-S3 (pins from config.example.h)
VCC 5 V
GND GND
TRIG GPIO 4 for the x sensor, GPIO 6 for the y sensor
ECHO GPIO 5 for the x sensor, GPIO 7 for the y sensor, each through the 1 kΩ + 2 kΩ divider

From the sensors to the browser

flowchart TD
    sx["<b>HC-SR04 on the Y axis</b><br/>measures x"]
    sy["<b>HC-SR04 on the X axis</b><br/>measures y"]
    esp["<b>ESP32-S3</b><br/>pings them in turn,<br/>~16 pairs per second"]
    srv["<b>server.py</b><br/>median + low-pass per sensor,<br/>mm to area pixels"]
    page["<b>Web page</b><br/>draws the trail,<br/>makes the 28×28 image"]
    nn["<b>server.py: /predict</b><br/>centre of mass,<br/>784 → 256 → 10 network"]
    sx -- echo time --> esp
    sy -- echo time --> esp
    esp -- "UDP over WiFi, text like 183 207" --> srv
    srv -- server-sent events --> page
    page -- "784 pixels, 4 s after the first point" --> nn
    nn -- "label + 10 probabilities" --> page
    classDef learnt fill:#2563eb22,stroke:#2563eb,stroke-width:2px
    class nn learnt

The ESP32 sends each pair of distances as one UDP packet of plain text, such as 183 207, with -1 for a sensor that heard no echo. UDP suits this: a lost packet is one missing point, and a late point is worse than none, so there is nothing worth sending again.

On the computer, server.py does three things with each packet.

It smooths each sensor. A still object doesn’t give a still reading: on my bench, consecutive readings of an object that didn’t move differed by 5.9 mm on average. Two filters fix most of it. A median of the last three readings drops a single bad ping, a spike or a missing echo. Then a low-pass filter, an exponential moving average, evens out the jitter that is left:

\[\hat{x}_k = \hat{x}_{k-1} + \alpha\,(m_k - \hat{x}_{k-1}), \qquad \alpha = 0.5\]

where \(m_k\) is the median of the latest three readings and \(\hat{x}_k\) the smoothed value.

class Smoother:
    def __init__(self, median_of, low_pass):
        self.recent = deque(maxlen=median_of)
        self.weight = low_pass
        self.avg = None

    def __call__(self, reading):
        self.recent.append(reading)
        median = sorted(self.recent)[len(self.recent) // 2]
        if median < 0:
            self.avg = None
            return -1
        self.avg = median if self.avg is None else self.avg + self.weight * (median - self.avg)
        return round(self.avg)

The repo’s self-test feeds it these readings, in mm:

Readings 100 100 900 100 −1 100 −1 −1
Median of 3 100 100 100 100 100 100 −1 −1

The 900 mm spike and the single missing echo vanish. Two missing echoes in a row get through, because then the object really is gone.

Readings 100 200 200 −1 300
Low-pass, α = 0.5 100 150 175 −1 300

The low-pass moves halfway to each new reading, and starts over after a missing echo so that the next trail doesn’t drift in from where the last one ended.

Together they cut the average step between readings of a still object from 5.9 to 2.0 mm. Neither is free. The median of three delays the point by one reading, about 60 ms, and the low-pass with α = 0.5 needs three readings to cover seven eighths of a sudden move. Both are set in config.toml (median_of, low_pass), and changing them while drawing is the quickest way to feel the trade between noise and lag.

It maps millimetres to the drawing area. The area is 480×480 px on the page. Distances between \(x_0 = 150\) and \(x_1 = 250\) mm map to 0–480 px from left to right, and the same for y, flipped, because y grows upwards on the apparatus and downwards on a screen:

\[p_x = \frac{x - x_0}{x_1 - x_0}\,W, \qquad p_y = \left(1 - \frac{y - y_0}{y_1 - y_0}\right) H\]

It relays the point to every open page over server-sent events: one long HTTP response that the browser reads line by line with EventSource.

Drawing in the air

My first try at drawing with the sensors felt wrong in two ways. The dot jumped from reading to reading, 16 times a second, and I couldn’t tell how big the area was or where its edges were. The Ultrasonic tab now deals with both.

Left: mid-stroke, the dot glides from one reading to the next and the trail follows it. Right: the pen left the area through the bottom; a ring waits on the edge and the text says how far to move back.
  • The dot glides. Between two readings the dot moves in a straight line over the measured time between packets, and the trail is drawn as curves through the midpoints of its points instead of straight segments. Sixteen points a second then look like motion.
  • The edges are in millimetres. The scale around the area matches the distances in config.toml, and the line under the title shows both live readings.
  • Leaving the area lifts the pen. Outside the area the trail breaks, a ring stays on the nearest edge and the page says which way and how far to move back. Leaving is also how you start the next digit: after a read, a new trail starts only when the pen has left the area and come back.
  • The network sees the area as drawn, without rescaling. More on this in From trail to input.

The network

The page’s third tab, Model, describes the network that reads the digits. It reads everything from the model file, so it follows each retraining. This section goes through it in more depth.

The top of the Model tab: the headline numbers, the layers and the accuracy after each epoch.

The dataset: MNIST

The first three test images of each digit in MNIST, enlarged from 28×28 pixels.

MNIST (LeCun, Cortes and Burges, 1998) has 70,000 handwritten digits: 60,000 for training and 10,000 for testing, written by US Census Bureau employees and high-school students, with different writers in the two sets. Each digit was scaled to fit a 20×20 box, anti-aliased to grey levels, and placed in a 28×28 image with its centre of mass in the middle. train.py downloads the four files from a Google Cloud mirror and reads them with NumPy alone:

def load_mnist(split):
    """Images as (n, 784) float32 in 0..1, labels as (n,) int."""
    prefix = "train" if split == "train" else "t10k"
    out = []
    for name, offset in ((f"{prefix}-images-idx3-ubyte.gz", 16), (f"{prefix}-labels-idx1-ubyte.gz", 8)):
        path = DATA / name
        if not path.exists():
            DATA.mkdir(exist_ok=True)
            urllib.request.urlretrieve(URL + name, path)
        out.append(np.frombuffer(gzip.decompress(path.read_bytes()), np.uint8, offset=offset))
    images, labels = out
    return images.reshape(-1, 784).astype(np.float32) / 255, labels.astype(int)

The offsets skip each file’s header, 16 bytes for images and 8 for labels. Everything after it is one byte per pixel or per label.

From trail to input

A network only knows the kind of image it was trained on, so the page turns a trail into an image the way MNIST digits were made:

  1. The whole drawing area shrinks to 28×28. The 10 cm area becomes 28 pixels, 3.6 mm each, and the dashed box on it is the 20×20 box MNIST digits fill. A digit keeps the size it was drawn at.
  2. The trail is drawn white on black with a 2.5 px line, about the stroke width of an MNIST digit. The thick trail on screen plays no part.
  3. The server moves the centre of mass to the middle, as MNIST did.
  4. The 784 pixel values, from 0 to 1, go through the network.

The first two steps are a canvas transform in the page (simplified from rasterize()):

const scale = 28 / Math.max(W, H);  // area px to network px
small.setTransform(scale, 0, 0, scale, 14 - scale * W / 2, 14 - scale * H / 2);
small.strokeStyle = '#fff';
small.lineWidth = cfg.inference.stroke_width / scale;
strokePaths(small);

The third is a few lines of NumPy on the server:

def center_of_mass(img):
    """Shift a 28x28 image so its center of mass sits in the middle, as MNIST does."""
    total = img.sum()
    if total == 0:
        return img
    ys, xs = np.indices(img.shape)
    dy, dx = round(13.5 - (ys * img).sum() / total), round(13.5 - (xs * img).sum() / total)
    return np.roll(img, (dy, dx), axis=(0, 1))

At first the page scaled each trail to fill MNIST’s box, as MNIST did with each digit. That reads well, but it hides the space you are drawing in: with the sensors I couldn’t tell how big I was writing, and whatever I drew, the network got the same size. With the fixed frame, the dashed box says how big to write, and the 28×28 preview fills in live as you draw, so you see what the network will get. fit_box = true in config.toml brings back the per-trail scaling to compare.

The architecture

It’s a multilayer perceptron with one hidden layer of 256 units:

\[\mathbf{h} = \max(0,\; \mathbf{x} W_1 + \mathbf{b}_1), \qquad \mathbf{z} = \mathbf{h} W_2 + \mathbf{b}_2, \qquad p_i = \frac{e^{z_i}}{\sum_j e^{z_j}}\]

Here \(\mathbf{x}\) is the image as a row of 784 numbers. Each hidden unit takes a weighted sum of all 784 pixels and keeps it if it is positive (ReLU). Each output takes a weighted sum of the 256 hidden units, and the softmax turns the 10 outputs into probabilities that add up to 1. The answer is the digit with the highest one.

Layer Weights Biases Parameters
Input → hidden 784 × 256 = 200,704 256 200,960
Hidden → output 256 × 10 = 2,560 10 2,570
Network     203,530

The whole forward pass is four lines. Subtracting the largest output before the exponential gives the same softmax and keeps np.exp from overflowing:

def forward(model, x):
    h = np.maximum(0, x @ model["W1"] + model["b1"])
    z = h @ model["W2"] + model["b2"]
    e = np.exp(z - z.max(axis=1, keepdims=True))
    return h, e / e.sum(axis=1, keepdims=True)

Training: backpropagation by hand

No framework computes the gradients here; they are written out. For one image with true label \(y\), the loss is the cross-entropy, minus the log of the probability given to the right answer:

\[L = -\log p_y\]

Its gradient with respect to the outputs before the softmax, \(\mathbf{z}\), comes out short: the predicted probabilities minus the one-hot true label.

\[\frac{\partial L}{\partial \mathbf{z}} = \mathbf{p} - \mathbf{e}_y\]

From there the chain rule runs backwards through each layer. ReLU passes the gradient where the unit was active and blocks it where it wasn’t:

\[\frac{\partial L}{\partial W_2} = \mathbf{h}^\top (\mathbf{p} - \mathbf{e}_y), \qquad \boldsymbol{\delta}_h = \big((\mathbf{p} - \mathbf{e}_y)\, W_2^\top\big) \odot [\mathbf{h} > 0], \qquad \frac{\partial L}{\partial W_1} = \mathbf{x}^\top \boldsymbol{\delta}_h\]

Each weight then takes a small step against its gradient, \(W \leftarrow W - \eta\, \partial L / \partial W\), with learning rate \(\eta = 0.1\) and the gradient averaged over a mini-batch of 100 images. In code:

for epoch in range(epochs):
    order = rng.permutation(len(x))
    for i in range(0, len(x), batch):
        xb, yb = x[order[i:i + batch]], y[order[i:i + batch]]
        h, p = forward(model, xb)
        dz = p
        dz[np.arange(len(yb)), yb] -= 1  # softmax + cross-entropy gradient
        dz /= len(yb)
        dh = (dz @ model["W2"].T) * (h > 0)
        model["W2"] -= lr * h.T @ dz
        model["b2"] -= lr * dz.sum(axis=0)
        model["W1"] -= lr * xb.T @ dh
        model["b1"] -= lr * dh.sum(axis=0)

The weights start random, drawn from a normal distribution with \(\sigma = \sqrt{2 / n_\text{in}}\) (He initialisation), which keeps the signal from fading or blowing up as it passes through ReLU units. Ten passes over the 60,000 images take 11.3 seconds on a CPU.

What the hidden units learnt

Each hidden unit has one input weight per pixel, so its 784 weights can be drawn as a 28×28 image.

Eight hidden units picked at random. Top: each unit's 784 input weights. Bottom: the same weights minus their random starting values, which is what training added. Blue pixels push the unit on when there is ink on them, orange ones push it off. Each tile is scaled to its own largest weight.

The top row is mostly noise, and that is a lesson in itself. A pixel that is black in every training image adds nothing to \(\partial L / \partial W_1 = \mathbf{x}^\top \boldsymbol{\delta}_h\), so its weights never move: 67 of the 784 pixels are never inked in MNIST’s training set, and their weights are exactly what the random start gave them. Elsewhere, training changed the weights by about 0.02 (root mean square), against starting values of about 0.05. The random start is still most of what you see.

train.py seeds its random generator, so the start can be recomputed and subtracted. What’s left in the bottom row is what was learnt: strokes, arcs and loops in different places, blue where ink should be and orange where it shouldn’t. Each unit detects one such pattern, and the output layer learns which combinations of them make a 7.

Training results

Train accuracy is measured on the images the network learns from, and test accuracy on 10,000 it never sees. If train accuracy kept rising while test accuracy stalled, the network would be memorising its training images instead of learning digits: overfitting. Here the gap stays under one point, so this small network isn’t overfitting much yet.

The confusion matrix shows which mistakes it makes. Rows are the true digit and columns what the network read, so the diagonal holds the correct reads and every other cell is an error. 246 of the 10,000 test digits were misread. The biggest cells are pairs that share most of their strokes: 4 and 7 read as 9, 13 times each, 2 read as 8 (11) and 9 read as 4 (10). 0 and 1 are read best, 99.0% each, and 7 worst, 96.4%.

Train your own symbol

The page only reads; it never trains. To teach the network a new symbol, a letter or your own way of writing a digit:

  1. Draw at least 30 images of each symbol, varying size, slant and position. Any size and any format Pillow reads will do, dark on a light background or light on black.
  2. Put them in a folder named after the label: 
    data/custom/
├── A/
│   ├── 001.png
│   └── ...
├── plus/
│   └── ...
└── 7/          your own 7s, added to MNIST's
  3. Run python3 train.py (it needs pip install pillow for this) and restart server.py.

train.py crops each image to its symbol, scales it into a 20×20 box and centres it in 28×28: the MNIST recipe again. Labels that aren’t digits become extra outputs after 0–9. Every fifth image of each label is held out for testing. A few dozen images would be drowned out by MNIST’s ~6,000 per digit, so each label is oversampled to 1,000 copies, each shifted by up to 2 pixels:

for c in np.unique(cy[~ctest]):
    pick = rng.choice(np.flatnonzero((cy == c) & ~ctest), 1000)
    shifts = rng.integers(-2, 3, (1000, 2))
    copies = [np.roll(cx[i].reshape(28, 28), s, axis=(0, 1)).ravel() for i, s in zip(pick, shifts)]
    x, y = np.concatenate([x, copies]), np.concatenate([y, np.full(1000, c)])

A symbol unlike any digit, such as + or X, learns well from a few dozen images. One that looks like a digit (O and 0, l and 1, S and 5) gets confused with it, and the confusion matrix on the Model tab shows how often. For a whole alphabet, a dataset such as EMNIST Letters beats drawing hundreds of samples by hand.

Teaching with it

Electronics and machine learning are usually taught in separate rooms. Here one depends on the other: the network can only be as good as the readings, and the readings only matter because something reads them.

The practical side

Each part gives students something to build, break and measure:

Part What it teaches Something to try
HC-SR04 Time of flight, speed of sound Measure a known distance and solve for the speed of sound
Echo divider Logic levels, voltage dividers Measure ECHO before and after the divider with a multimeter or a scope
Two sensors Crosstalk, timing budgets Set PING_GAP_MS to 0 and look for one sensor hearing the other’s ping
WiFi and UDP IP addresses, ports, firewalls, lost packets Watch the readings per second in the page’s top bar while carrying the board away from the router
server.py Median and low-pass filters, lag Draw the same digit with low_pass at 1.0, 0.5 and 0.2
The page Sampling, interpolation, rasterisation Draw a digit half the size of the dashed box, then again with fit_box = true
train.py Datasets, backpropagation, overfitting Change hidden from 256 to 16 or 1024 and compare accuracy and training time

The theoretical side

The same parts lead to questions that can be worked out on paper:

  • Measurement error has many sources. The speed of sound changes with temperature, roughly \(v \approx 331.3 + 0.606\,T\) m/s with \(T\) in °C. With the firmware’s 343 m/s (20 °C) in a 30 °C room, an object at 203.5 mm reads as 200 mm.
  • A distance is not a coordinate. Each sensor reports the distance to the object, not its position along the sensor’s axis. An object off the axis by an angle \(\theta\) reads \(x / \cos\theta\): at the edge of a 15° beam (\(\theta = 7.5^\circ\)) that is 0.9% long, about 1.7 mm at 200 mm. It’s the same geometry behind every range sensor.
  • Filters trade noise for lag, and the trade can be computed. After a sudden move, an exponential average with weight \(\alpha\) still lacks \((1-\alpha)^n\) of it after \(n\) readings.
  • Resolution has limits at both ends. The sensors give a point about every 60 ms, and the network sees the 10 cm area as 28 pixels of 3.6 mm. A digit drawn too fast has few points; one drawn too small covers a handful of pixels.
  • Training data defines what a model can do. MNIST is pen on paper. Air-drawn trails are smoother, have a constant width and shake in their own way. Making the input look like MNIST (the same box, the same stroke width, the centre of mass in the middle) is most of what makes the network work here. When it fails, asking how the input differs from the training set usually finds the reason.
  • Backpropagation is the chain rule. With a dozen lines of NumPy there is no framework between the student and the math, and each gradient in the code can be checked against a finite difference.

Exercises

  1. Measure the speed of sound in the room with one sensor and a ruler, and compare it with \(331.3 + 0.606\,T\).
  2. Write the same digit with the smoothing off (median_of = 1, low_pass = 1.0) and on, and describe the difference in the trail.
  3. Check one gradient in train.py with a finite difference: nudge one weight by \(10^{-4}\), and compare the change in the loss with the gradient times \(10^{-4}\).
  4. Train with 16, 64, 256 and 1024 hidden units, and plot test accuracy and training time against the number of parameters.
  5. Teach the network a + sign from 30 drawings and read its row of the confusion matrix.
  6. Replace the hidden layer with a small convolutional network and compare. An MLP treats every pixel position on its own; a convolution reuses the same small filters everywhere.

What it cannot do yet

  • The rig isn’t finished. The board reads both sensors and streams them to the page, but on my bench the sensor measuring y gets no echo yet, so the area isn’t calibrated. The air-drawn digits in this post come from a script that sends traced points as UDP packets, the same way the ESP32 does.
  • The area is small. Both beams have to see the object, which leaves a 10 cm square 15–25 cm from the sensors. A thin object, such as a pen tip or a finger, works best.
  • It’s slow. About 16 points a second, so a digit written in under a second has too few of them.
  • It measures distances, not coordinates. The error is small in the middle of the area and grows towards its edges.

Try it at my repo

It needs Python 3.11+ and NumPy:

python3 train.py      # downloads MNIST to data/, trains the network, writes model.npz
python3 server.py     # then open http://127.0.0.1:8000

The Mouse tab works without any hardware: draw a digit that fills the dashed box and wait four seconds. For the sensors, copy firmware/config.example.h to firmware/config.h, fill in your WiFi network and your computer’s address, flash it to an ESP32-S3 and open the Ultrasonic tab. The README has the wiring and the flashing steps.
entry.summary: Two HC-SR04 sensors, an ESP32 and a small network written in NumPy turn a pen moving through the air into a digit, and each step is small enough to teach.

entry.title: Measuring how long robotics journals take to review papers

link.title: Measuring how long robotics journals take to review papers

entry.content:
Why review time deserves data

Picking a journal is a bet on time. A PhD student with a defense date, a postdoc on the job market, or a lab with a grant report due all need to know one thing: how long until this paper is accepted?

The usual answers are folklore. A labmate’s story, a forum thread, or the “average time to first decision” a publisher puts on its homepage, which leaves out revision rounds. The real numbers already exist. Many journals print “Received / Accepted” dates on every paper. Nobody collects them in one place for the venues you are actually choosing between.

Paper Stats is a small tool that collects them for you.

What Paper Stats does

You give it a list of journals and a year range. It returns, for each journal, how many days papers spent between “received” and “accepted”, as a box plot, a summary table and a CSV.

It works in three steps:

  • Find papers. It asks arXiv for recent preprints whose authors tagged them with the journal’s name, and takes each one’s DOI.
  • Get the dates. It looks up each DOI in Crossref, the registry behind DOIs. Some publishers deposit the full article history there. For the others, it reads the “Manuscript received …; accepted …” footnote on the first page of the arXiv PDF.
  • Summarize. It reports the median and interquartile range per journal, sorted fastest first, and links every data point to its paper so you can check it.

Every number traces back to a date the journal printed. When no such date exists, the tool says so instead of guessing.

How it works

%%{init: {"flowchart": {"wrappingWidth": 320}}}%%
flowchart TD
    arxiv["<b>Search arXiv</b><br/>Preprints tagged with<br/>the journal + DOI"]
    crossref["<b>Look up the DOI in Crossref</b><br/>Checks the venue,<br/>gets the publication date"]
    pdf["<b>Read page 1 of the arXiv PDF</b><br/>“Manuscript received …;<br/>accepted …”"]
    proxy["<b>Proxy only</b><br/>arXiv v1 → journal publication,<br/>plotted apart"]
    mcross["<b>Measured: Crossref history</b><br/>Deposited by<br/>Springer and Wiley"]
    mpdf["<b>Measured: PDF footnote</b><br/>Mostly IEEE final versions"]
    arxiv --> crossref
    crossref -- no dates --> pdf
    crossref -- has dates --> mcross
    pdf -- no dates --> proxy
    pdf -- dates found --> mpdf
    classDef measured fill:#2563eb22,stroke:#2563eb,stroke-width:2px
    classDef fallback stroke-dasharray:6 4
    class mcross,mpdf measured
    class proxy fallback

Each paper goes down the left column until a step finds its dates. Crossref also drops papers whose venue doesn’t match the journal. Without that check, a search for Robotics and Autonomous Systems also pulls in Annual Review of Control, Robotics, and Autonomous Systems.

The two measured sources are trusted the same: both are dates the publisher printed. The proxy is kept for journals that print nothing, but it is drawn as a separate box in every chart and never averaged with the real numbers.

What a run found

I ran it on 12 robotics and automation journals, asking for 25 papers each published in 2022–2026. It kept 189 papers, and 69 of them had printed review dates: 36 from Crossref and 33 from PDF footnotes.

With 10 to 16 papers per journal, read this as a first look, not a ranking. The spread matters as much as the median: at Journal of Field Robotics, the middle half of papers took anywhere from about 6 to 15 months.

Two results argue for using printed dates instead of arXiv dates:

  • Many authors post after acceptance. Of the 36 papers dated through Crossref, 9 went on arXiv only after they were accepted. arXiv’s own timestamps say nothing about their review.
  • The arXiv proxy misses in both directions. Measured from first arXiv version to publication, Autonomous Robots looks like 638 days (measured review: 266) and RA-L like 92 days (measured: 133).

Who it is for

  • PhD students and postdocs. When a thesis defense or a job application needs the paper accepted by a set date, the median and spread show which journals can realistically make it.
  • Supervisors. It is a quick, sourced answer to “where should this go?” that you can show a student, instead of “in my experience”.
  • Editors and editorial boards. It benchmarks your journal against the ones authors actually compare it with, using your own printed dates.
  • Meta-researchers. The CSV holds per-paper dates and sources, ready to analyze, and the method is written up as a flowchart for a methodology section.

The journal list is a text file. Swap the robotics titles for your own field and the same pipeline runs.

What it cannot tell you

  • It only sees papers on arXiv. Labs that don’t post preprints, or don’t fill in the journal reference, are invisible to it. Accepted papers are also the only ones that ever get a “received” date, so rejections never show up.
  • Coverage depends on the publisher. SAGE and Elsevier deposit no review dates in Crossref, and their preprints rarely carry them. For journals like IJRR and Robotics and Autonomous Systems, the tool falls back to the proxy. IEEE dates appear only when authors upload the final version: 16 of 25 RA-L papers had them, but only 2 of 25 T-RO papers.
  • “Received” can reset. Some journals restart the clock after a reject-and-resubmit, so the printed time understates the real wait.
  • The proxy is a rough bound. arXiv v1 to journal publication is short or negative when authors post after acceptance, and long when they post years before submitting. It is never mixed into the measured numbers.
  • Samples are recent-first. Each journal’s sample is its latest N usable papers, not a random draw over the year range.

Try it at my repo

It is a small Python app with two dependencies, Flask and pypdf:

python3 -m venv venv
venv/bin/pip install -r requirements.txt
venv/bin/python server.py

Open http://127.0.0.1:5000, put your journals in list_of_journals.txt, set the sample size and year range in the Configuration tab, and press Fetch Data & Run Analysis.

The first run takes a while, because arXiv asks clients to wait 3 seconds between requests and the tool respects that. For the 12 journals above it took 32 minutes. Every lookup is cached, so the rerun took under 2 minutes. When it finishes, download the CSV and check any number against its paper.

If your field’s journals print dates in a format the parser misses, the matching rules are a few lines in collector.py, with tests next to them.
entry.summary: Paper Stats collects the received and accepted dates journals print, so you can pick a venue on data instead of folklore.

entry.title: Understanding Rating Systems
entry.content:
In the world of competitive games and sports, rating systems play a crucial role in measuring player or team skill levels, predicting match outcomes, and facilitating fair matchmaking. Among the most influential are the Elo rating system and its successors, Glicko and Glicko-2. These systems, rooted in statistical models, help quantify relative strengths in zero-sum games like chess, esports, and even traditional sports. In this blog post, we’ll dive deep into how each system works, explore their mathematical foundations with equations, and examine real-world applications, including their specific use in Dota 2 for player MMR and team rankings. Whether you’re a data enthusiast, a gamer, or a sports analyst, understanding these can shed light on why your favorite team ranks where it does.

The Elo Rating System

The Elo rating system, named after its creator Arpad Elo, a Hungarian-American physicist and chess master, was developed in the mid-20th century as an improvement over earlier methods like the Harkness system. It assumes that player performance is a normally distributed random variable, with the mean representing true skill inferred from wins, losses, and draws. Adopted by the United States Chess Federation (USCF) in 1960 and the World Chess Federation (FIDE) in 1970, Elo’s method is self-correcting: points are transferred from the loser to the winner, ensuring ratings reflect relative strengths within a pool.

Core Mathematics of Elo

At its heart, Elo predicts the expected outcome of a match based on rating differences and updates ratings accordingly.

  • Expected Score Calculation: For two players A and B with ratings $ R_A $ and $ R_B $, the expected score $ E_A $ for player A (probability of winning, plus half a draw) is given by the logistic function:

    \[E_A = \frac{1}{1 + 10^{(R_B - R_A)/400}}\]

    Similarly, $ E_B = 1 - E_A $. The factor 400 is chosen so that a 400-point difference implies the higher-rated player has about a 91% chance of winning. An alternative formulation uses:

    \[E_A = \frac{Q_A}{Q_A + Q_B}, \quad \text{where} \quad Q_A = 10^{R_A/400}, \quad Q_B = 10^{R_B/400}\]

  • Rating Update: After the game, player A’s new rating $ R_A’ $ is:

    \[R_A' = R_A + K \cdot (S_A - E_A)\]

    Here, $ S_A $ is the actual score (1 for win, 0.5 for draw, 0 for loss), and $ K $ is the “K-factor,” which controls the magnitude of changes. Higher K values (e.g., 40 for new players) allow rapid adjustments, while lower ones (e.g., 10 for experts) stabilize ratings. Organizations like FIDE vary K based on rating and games played, such as $ K = 40 $ for beginners and $ K = 10 $ for those rated 2400+.

The USCF uses a dynamic K: $ K = \frac{800}{N_e + m} $, where $ N_e $ is the effective number of games rated, and $ m $ is games in the current tournament.

Real-World Applications of Elo

Originally designed for chess, Elo has expanded far beyond. In esports, it’s used for matchmaking in games like League of Legends (pre-Season 2), Overwatch (with seasonal adjustments), and Classic Tetris. It powers global power rankings, capturing regional strengths like NA vs. EU in League of Legends. In traditional sports, FIFA adopted Elo for men’s and women’s world rankings since 2018, and it’s applied to American college football (via BCS from 1998–2013), Major League Baseball (by analyst Nate Silver), tennis (Universal Tennis Rating), and even chess boxing (requiring a minimum 1600 Elo for pros). Extensions incorporate margin of victory for more nuanced rankings in team sports. Its predictive power makes it superior for dynamic rankings, as seen in sports analytics where it evaluates dominance across fields like hockey or baseball.

Glicko and Glicko-2 Rating Systems

Developed by statistician Mark Glickman in 1995, the Glicko system addresses Elo’s limitations by incorporating “Ratings Deviation” (RD), a measure of rating reliability that increases with inactivity or inconsistent play. Glicko-2, an extension, adds “volatility” (σ) to model expected performance fluctuations. Both are public domain and assume ratings evolve over time, performing best with 5–10 games per rating period.

Key Differences from Elo

Unlike Elo, which treats all ratings as equally reliable, Glicko uses RD to dampen updates when uncertainty is high (e.g., after long breaks). Glicko-2 further refines this with volatility, assuming strengths follow an auto-regressive normal process. This makes Glicko systems more adaptive for players with varying activity levels.

Mathematics of Glicko

  • RD Update (Pre-Games): RD increases over time:

    \[RD = \min\left(\sqrt{RD_0^2 + c^2 t}, 350\right)\]

    where $ t $ is rating periods elapsed, and $ c \approx 34.6 $ (tuned so RD reaches 350 after ~100 periods).

  • Rating Update (Post-Games): For $ m $ games, new rating $ r $:

    \[r = r_0 + \frac{q}{\frac{1}{RD^2} + \frac{1}{d^2}} \sum_{i=1}^{m} g(RD_i)(s_i - E(s|r_0, r_i, RD_i))\]

    with $ q = \frac{\ln(10)}{400} $, $ g(RD_i) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{1 + \frac{3q^2(RD_i^2)}{\pi^2}}} $, and expected score $ E $ similar to Elo but adjusted by $ g $. Then, $ d^2 $ is the inverse of a sum involving variances, and new RD is $ RD’ = \sqrt{\left(\frac{1}{RD^2} + \frac{1}{d^2}\right)^{-1}} $.

Mathematics of Glicko-2

Glicko-2 builds on this with volatility. Key steps include computing variance $ v $ and delta $ \Delta $:

\[v = \left[\sum_{j=1}^{m} g(\phi_j)^2 E(\mu, \mu_j, \phi_j)\{1 - E(\mu, \mu_j, \phi_j)\}\right]^{-1}\] \[\Delta = v \sum_{j=1}^{m} g(\phi_j)\{s_j - E(\mu, \mu_j, \phi_j)\}\]

where $ \phi $ is RD (scaled), $ \mu $ is rating, and functions $ g $ and $ E $ are analogous. Updates then incorporate σ for more precise volatility adjustments.

Real-World Applications of Glicko and Glicko-2

Glicko shines in online environments with irregular play. It’s used on chess platforms like Lichess and Chess.com, where RD stabilizes ratings for infrequent players. In esports, datDota employs Glicko-2 for Dota 2 team rankings, and Counter-Strike: Global Offensive (CS:GO) uses a variant for ranks, analyzing how volatility affects progression. Other games like Guild Wars 2 and World of Warcraft (pre-Elo shift) leverage it for matchmaking. Beyond gaming, adaptations evaluate sprinting performance in athletics or rank teams in volleyball and golf, treating matches as simultaneous for individual sports. Glicko-2’s team abstractions extend to multiplayer scenarios, motivating competitive play through accurate ladders.

Comparing Elo, Glicko, and Glicko-2

Elo is simple and effective for consistent competitors but ignores uncertainty. Glicko adds RD for better handling of inactivity, while Glicko-2’s volatility makes it ideal for volatile performances. In practice, Elo suits stable environments like professional chess, whereas Glicko variants excel in dynamic online games.

Rating Systems in Dota 2

While the core principles of Elo, Glicko, and Glicko-2 provide a universal framework for skill assessment, their adaptations in specific games like Dota 2 highlight how these systems evolve to meet the demands of massive multiplayer online battle arena (MOBA) environments. Dota 2, developed by Valve, has undergone significant changes to its matchmaking rating (MMR) system over the years, balancing competitive integrity, player retention, and computational efficiency. This section explores how Dota 2 has implemented (and iterated on) these systems for individual players and professional teams, drawing from historical transitions up to the current landscape in September 2025. We’ll focus on MMR evolution for players and third-party team rankings, as Valve does not maintain an official team MMR.

Player MMR: From Elo-Like Foundations to Glicko-Driven Matchmaking

Dota 2’s matchmaking system, which pairs players for fair games, has always been inspired by Elo’s zero-sum transfer of points based on expected vs. actual outcomes. Early iterations (pre-2013) used a basic Elo variant, where MMR was a hidden integer value starting around 1500, adjusted by a fixed amount per win/loss (typically ±25 MMR). This mirrored the Elo update equation:

\[R' = R + K (S - E)\]

with K often fixed at 32–40, leading to issues like MMR deflation (ratings drifting downward over time due to inconsistent play) and poor handling of new or inactive players.

By 2023, with Patch 7.33, Valve overhauled the system to adopt Glicko, a more sophisticated Bayesian approach that incorporates rating deviation (RD) to account for uncertainty. This shift addressed Elo’s limitations, such as over-penalizing streaks or failing to adjust for inactivity. Glicko estimates not just a player’s rating (μ) but also its reliability via RD (φ), which widens with fewer games, reducing the impact of outliers. The expected score E now factors in RD:

\[E = \frac{1}{\sqrt{1 + 3 q^2 \phi^2 / \pi^2}} \cdot \frac{1}{1 + 10^{(r_j - r_i)/400}}\]

where q = ln(10)/400, and the g(φ) term dampens predictions for uncertain ratings. Post-match updates use a variance-weighted adjustment, converging faster for active players while stabilizing veterans.

As of September 2025, Dota 2’s player MMR remains Glicko-based, integrated into a seasonal ranking structure introduced in 2024. Seasons reset medals (e.g., Herald to Immortal) but preserve hidden MMR, with visible tiers like:

Tier MMR Range (Season 6, Aug 2025)
Herald 1–769
Guardian 770–1539
Crusader 1540–2309
Archon 2310–3079
Legend 3080–3849
Ancient 3850–4619
Divine 4620–5389
Immortal 5390+

Wins grant 20–30+ MMR (factoring behavior score and party size), while losses deduct similarly, modulated by RD for “confidence” in the rating—low-confidence players see smaller swings. This prevents smurfing and rewards consistency, with ~1% of players in Immortal. Glicko also enables “calibration” matches for new accounts (10 games to set initial RD). Unlike full Glicko-2, Dota 2 omits explicit volatility (σ) to simplify for 10 million+ monthly users, though it implicitly handles variance through match history weighting.

The evolution has improved matchmaking quality: Pre-Glicko, MMR inflation/deflation skewed queues; now, RD ensures balanced games even for returning players. Community feedback in 2025 praises the system’s fairness, though debates persist on party MMR penalties.

Team Rankings: Glicko-2 in Professional Dota 2 via datDota

For professional teams, Valve relies on community tools like datDota for Glicko-2 ratings, as official MMR is player-centric. datDota, a leading analytics site, applies Glicko-2 to aggregate team performance from ~100,000 pro matches, treating teams as entities with shared volatility. This extends the player model by averaging individual MMRs and factoring series outcomes (Bo3/Bo5), incorporating RD for roster changes and meta shifts.

Glicko-2’s volatility (σ) is key here: It models how a team’s strength fluctuates with patches (e.g., 7.37 in early 2025 buffed carries, spiking underdog wins). Updates use the full formula:

\[\Delta = v \sum g(\phi_j) (s_j - E)\]

followed by σ and φ recalibration, with a rolling 6–12 month window for relevance. As of mid-2025, top teams like Team Falcons (1985+ Glicko-2) reflect post-TI dominance, with the event’s average rating hitting a record 1935.5—making it the “toughest LAN ever.”

These ratings inform bracket predictions, seeding, and betting, outperforming Elo in volatile metas. datDota’s variants (Glicko-1, Elo-32/64) allow comparisons, but Glicko-2 is the gold standard for pros.

Why These Systems Matter in Dota 2

Dota 2’s adoption of Glicko for players and Glicko-2 for teams exemplifies iterative refinement: Elo provided the base, but uncertainty modeling via RD and σ ensures resilience against the game’s 120+ heroes, patches, and team dynamics. As of 2025, no major overhauls are announced, but seasonal tweaks continue to refine confidence intervals. For aspiring analysts or our Dota 2 prediction project, these systems form the backbone—feeding features like rating diffs into neural nets for ~65% accurate win probs.

entry.title: GraphSLAM Formulation
entry.content:
Introduction

\( ewcommand\x{\mathbf{x}} ewcommand\xk{\mathbf{x}_k} ewcommand\xkk{\mathbf{x}_{k+1}} ewcommand\Hessian{\mathbf{H}} ewcommand\I{\mathbf{I}} ewcommand\e{\mathbf{e}}\) In the context of SLAM, we aim to estimate the optimal poses of a robot and the locations of landmarks by minimizing the error between sensor measurements and their predicted values . The optimization seeks to find the configuration of robot poses and landmark locations that minimizes the sum of the squared errors.

Formally, consider a system with:

  • A set of $M$ measurements, or constraints in the graph. Each measurement $e_j \in \mathcal{E}$ is associated with:
    • An error vector $\mathbf{e}_j \in \mathbb{R}^{n_j}$, where $n_j$ is the dimensionality of the measurement error, which is dependent on the sensor type.
    • An information matrix $\Omega_j \in \mathbb{R}^{n_j imes n_j}$, representing the inverse covariance of the measurement noise.
  • A set of $N$ robot poses, or vertices in the graph, $\mathcal{V} = {v_1, \dots, v_N}$. Each pose $v_i \in \mathcal{V}$ is represented by a compact state vector $\x_i \in \mathbb{R}^c$, for the 3D case, $c = 6$ and $\x = egin{bmatrix}x,\; y,\; z,\; \phi,\; heta,\; \psi\end{bmatrix}^ op$.
  • A pose composition operator $ oxplus$ that combines pose increments $\Delta \x$ with an existing compact pose $\x$ to yield an updated (potentially non-compact) pose in $\mathbb{R}^d$ ($d eq c$) , the work of has a detailed explanation on this operation.

Our goal is to find the set of robot poses $\x = egin{bmatrix} \x_1, \x_2, \dots, \x_N \end{bmatrix}^{ op} \in \mathbb{R}^{cN}$ that minimizes the total squared error, the $\chi^2$ cost function: egin{align} \chi^2(\x) = \sum_{e_j \in \mathcal{E}} \mathbf{e}_j(\x)^ op \Omega_j \mathbf{e}_j(\x). \end{align}

Back-end Formulation

This optimization problem is typically non-linear and is solved iteratively using techniques such as Gauss-Newton (GN), Levenberg-Marquardt (LM) , Powell’s dogleg (PDL) or Graduated Non-Convexity (GNC) . Let $\xk$ be the estimate of the state vector at iteration $k$. We seek an update $\Delta \xk$ such that the updated state $\xkk = \xk oxplus \Delta \xk$ leads to a lower $\chi^2$ value.

To find this update, we linearize the error function $\e_j(\xkk)$ around the current estimate $\xk$: egin{align} \mathbf{e}_j(\xkk) &= \mathbf{e}_j(\xk oxplus \Delta \xk) ewline &\approx \mathbf{e}_j(\xk) + \mathbf{J}_j \Delta \xk, \end{align}

where \(\mathbf{J}_j = \left. rac{\partial \mathbf{e}_j(\xk oxplus \Delta \xk)}{\partial \Delta \xk} ight|_{\Delta \xk = \mathbf{0}}\) is the Jacobian matrix of the error function with respect to the state update. Using the chain rule, the Jacobian can be further decomposed as:

\[\mathbf{J}_j = \left( \left. rac{\partial \mathbf{e}_j(\xk oxplus \Delta \xk)}{\partial (\xk oxplus \Delta \xk)} ight|_{\Delta \xk = \mathbf{0}} ight) rac{\partial (\xk oxplus \Delta \xk)}{\partial \Delta \xk}.\]

Substituting the linearized error into the $\chi^2$ cost function, we get a quadratic approximation of the error around $\xk$:

\[ egin{align} &\chi^2(\xkk) \approx \sum_{e_j \in \mathcal{E}} (\mathbf{e}_j(\xk) + \mathbf{J}_j \Delta \xk)^ op \Omega_j (\mathbf{e}_j(\xk) + \mathbf{J}_j \Delta \xk) ewline &= \sum_{e_j \in \mathcal{E}} \left[ \mathbf{e}_j(\xk)^ op \Omega_j \mathbf{e}_j(\xk) + 2 \mathbf{e}_j(\xk)^ op \Omega_j \mathbf{J}_j \Delta \xk + (\Delta \xk)^ op \mathbf{J}_j^ op \Omega_j \mathbf{J}_j \Delta \xk ight] ewline &= \chi_k^2 + 2 \mathbf{b}^ op \Delta \xk + (\Delta \xk)^ op \Hessian \Delta \xk, \end{align}\]

where the gradient vector $\mathbf{b}$ and the Hessian matrix $\Hessian$ are defined as:

\[ egin{align} \mathbf{b}^ op = \sum_{e_j \in \mathcal{E}} \mathbf{e}_j(\xk)^ op \Omega_j \mathbf{J}_j ewline \Hessian = \sum_{e_j \in \mathcal{E}} \mathbf{J}_j^ op \Omega_j \mathbf{J}_j. \end{align}\]

To find the optimal update $\Delta \xk$ that minimizes this quadratic approximation, we set the derivative with respect to $\Delta \xk$ to zero:

egin{align} rac{\partial \chi^2(\xkk)}{\partial \Delta \xk} = 2 \mathbf{b} + 2 \Hessian \Delta \xk = 0.
\end{align}

Solving for $\Delta \xk$, we obtain the Gauss-Newton update rule: egin{align} \Delta \xk = -\Hessian^{-1} \mathbf{b}. \end{align}

This update is then applied to the current state estimate: $\xkk = \xk oxplus \Delta \xk$. This iterative process continues until convergence, yielding the optimized robot poses and potentially landmark locations that best explain the sensor data.

The GN optimization technique (derived above), can converge quickly, but it can also be unstable if the initial estimate is poor. LM acts as a bridge between the GN method and the gradient descent method. It introduces a damping factor $\lambda$ to the normal equation, $(\Hessian+\lambda \I)\Delta \xk=-\mathbf{b}$. When $\lambda$ is small, it behaves such as GN, but when large, it takes smaller, more cautious steps in the direction of the gradient, making it more robust than GN, especially with poor initial estimates. Similar to LM, the PDL method also combines Gauss-Newton with gradient descent but does so by operating within a “trust region”. It calculates both the GN update and the steepest-descent update and chooses an optimal step that remains within this trusted area, providing another robust alternative to pure GN .

Key aspects of this formulation include the error function, the information matrix and the Jacobian matrix. The structure of the Hessian matrix, often sparse in large-scale SLAM problems, is crucial for efficient computation of the optimal state estimate .

A significant challenge in real-world SLAM is the presence of outliers, such as false positive loop closures, that do not fit the model. The standard least-squares formulation is highly sensitive to outliers because the error is squared, causing a single bad measurement to have a disproportionately large influence on the final solution .

To mitigate this, the error function can be wrapped in a robust cost function, or kernel, $ ho(\cdot)$. The objective function becomes: egin{align} \chi^{2}(\x)=\sum_{\mathbf{e}_j \in \mathcal{E}} ho(\mathbf{e}_j^ op \Omega_j \mathbf{e}_j) \end{align}

The g2o framework provides several robust kernels, with the Huber kernel being one of the most common. The Huber function is quadratic for small errors but becomes linear for large errors. This means it penalizes outliers less severely than a standard quadratic function, preventing them from corrupting the entire optimization. A key advantage of the Huber kernel is that it remains convex, which means it does not introduce new local minima into the optimization problem, ensuring more stable convergence.

This function is designed to down-weight the influence of constraints with large errors, preventing them from corrupting the optimization . The g2o framework provides several such kernels, each with different properties, as shown in the figure below:

The Huber kernel is one of the most widely used robust functions. It behaves quadratically for small errors but switches to a linear function at a threshold $b$ for large errors, which prevents the error $e$ from being squared and amplified. Its formal definition is: egin{align} ho(e) = egin{cases} e^{2}, & ext{if } |e| \le b ewline 2b|e| - b^{2}, & ext{otherwise} \end{cases}. \end{align}

Geman-McClure is a non-convex kernel that more aggressively suppresses the influence of large errors. As the error $\e$ increases, the cost function flattens out and approaches a constant value $b$, effectively ignoring measurements that are considered strong outliers. Its formula is:
egin{align}
ho(e)= rac{ rac{e^{2}}{2}}{(b+e^{2})}. \end{align}

Dynamic Covariance Scaling (DCS) takes a different approach by introducing an additional scaling factor $s$ that directly modifies the information matrix for each loop closure constraint, as shown in the equation below. The scaling factor is close to 1 for inliers but drops towards zero for outliers, effectively down-rating their influence on the optimization . The scaling factor is defined as:
\( egin{align} \sum \mathbf{e}_{ ext{lc}}(\x)^ op (s^2 \Omega_{ ext{lc}}) \; \mathbf{e}_{ ext{lc}}(\x), ewline s = \min\Bigg(1, rac{2\Phi}{\Phi+\chi_{ ext{lc}}^2}\Bigg) \end{align}\)

where \(\mathbf{e}_{ ext{lc}}\) is the loop closure constraint, \(\Omega_{ ext{lc}}\) is the loop closure information matrix, $\Phi$ is a parameter defining the influence of the down-rate and $\chi_{ ext{lc}}^2$ is the original term for the loop closure constraint.

Other robust functions such as the Cauchy, Tukey, and Welsh kernels also exist, each offering a different non-convex strategy for down-weighting outliers. The choice of kernel is ultimately a trade-off between the desired level of robustness to extreme outliers and the stability of the optimization process. While non-convex kernels can offer better performance in the presence of severe outliers, convex options such as Huber are often preferred for their reliability and predictable behavior. Experiments show that robust kernels dramatically improve accuracy when initial estimates are poor or when data contains incorrect constraints .
